description:
FILED s452ab (Opus, round 11 agent AB) from the #734 probes.  PRE-EXISTING
(identical before and after that work) and unrelated to it.

    sub cxt { my $c = wantarray ? "list" : defined(wantarray) ? "scalar" : "void";
              return "printf '$c\n'" }
    print "bts=[", scalar(`${\ cxt() }`), "]\n";
        perl: bts=[list]        PCL: bts=[scalar]

`\ EXPR` propagates LIST context to EXPR (`\` applied to a list yields a list
of references), so a `${\ f() }` interpolation calls f in LIST context.  PCL
lowers the interpolated `${\ ...}` block with a SCALAR context.  Measured
inside a backtick body, but the mechanism is the interpolation of `${\ ...}`,
not the backtick: probe the same shape in a plain double-quoted string first.

The idiom matters because `${\ f() }` is the standard way to interpolate a
CALL into a string, and t/op/exec.t rows 31-32 use its literal form
(`${\"hello"}`, which is context-insensitive and works).

BAR: the row above in a dq string, in a backtick body and in a heredoc; the
list form `@{[ f() ]}` (which is already list context -- check it did not
regress); an f() that returns a LIST (perl takes the last ref); emission A/B.
subject: an interpolated backslash-ref block calls its EXPR in SCALAR context; perl propagates LIST context
